[Chapter 11 · Attention and the Transformer]{.eyebrow}

# Attention and Transformers

[Each token's new representation is a weighted average of the others, in the shape of the Nadaraya–Watson smoother the chapter introduces, with the similarity learned.]{.dek}
:::

The book reaches [attention]{.term} not as a novelty but as a return. To build the representation of a token, attention takes a weighted average of value vectors, with the weights set by how similar a query is to each key. That is the shape of the Nadaraya–Watson estimator, the classical kernel-weighted average, with two changes: the notion of similarity is now learned rather than fixed, and the weights are normalized by a softmax. The book is careful that the analogy does not need a kernel of the Chapter 8 kind: the attention kernel need not be symmetric, because the query and key projections can differ. The notebook makes the mechanism concrete by tracing exact values through the computation rather than drawing arrows between boxes.

Why gather context at all? Consider the word "bank" in "I deposited money at the bank" and "we sat by the river bank." The meaning depends on the surrounding words, so a good representation must incorporate them. Attention gives each position a way to pull information from every other position in proportion to relevance.

## Scaled dot-product attention

Each input is projected three ways. The [query]{.term} asks what this position is looking for, the [key]{.term} advertises what each position contains, and the [value]{.term} carries the information each position contributes. Scoring a query against every key by dot product, scaling, and passing through a softmax yields a probability distribution over positions; the output is the weighted average of the values.

::: {.defbox}
[Scaled Dot-Product Attention]{.lbl}

[ Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QK<sup>&#8868;</sup> / &radic;d<sub>k</sub> ) V ]{.math}
:::

```{=html}

<img src="../figures/ch11_01_attention_transformers.png?v=321331de" alt="Nine-by-nine heatmap of attention weights over a nine-token sentence; rows are the attending token, columns the token attended to. Most of the grid is pale, with a scatter of darker cells marking the links. The darkest is the pronoun row it against the column cat.">
<figcaption><strong>Where each token looks.</strong> One head of self-attention over a nine-token sentence, with the embeddings hand-built so the pattern is legible. Each row is a probability distribution across the columns. The pronoun <em>it</em> puts 0.63 on <em>cat</em>, its referent; the two <em>the</em> rows are identical, because nothing in the computation yet knows where a token sits. This is the result the code below reproduces.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

Read this beside the Nadaraya–Watson estimator and the kinship is unmistakable. The softmax term is exactly a vector of kernel weights, and multiplying by V is the weighted average those weights define. The only thing learned is the set of projections that produce Q, K, and V, which is to say the similarity metric itself.

## The book's house example

The book introduces the estimator with a house price. To price a 75 m&sup2; house from three sold houses of 60, 80 and 120 m&sup2;, priced at 420, 510 and 700 thousand euros, a kernel that falls with distance might give the weights 0.4, 0.5 and 0.1. In attention's terms the new house is the query, the sold houses' sizes are the keys, and their prices are the values.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

query  = 75                             # the new house, m^2
keys   = np.array([60, 80, 120])        # sold houses' sizes, m^2
values = np.array([420, 510, 700])      # their prices, thousand euros
w      = np.array([0.4, 0.5, 0.1])      # the book's weights: larger where the house is closer

print("distance to query:", np.abs(keys - query))
print("weights sum to", w.sum())
print("estimate:", w @ values, "thousand euros")   # the book: 493
```

## R
```{webr}
query  <- 75                            # the new house, m^2
keys   <- c(60, 80, 120)                # sold houses' sizes, m^2
values <- c(420, 510, 700)              # their prices, thousand euros
w      <- c(0.4, 0.5, 0.1)              # the book's weights: larger where the house is closer

cat("distance to query:", abs(keys - query), "\n")
cat("weights sum to", sum(w), "\n")
cat("estimate:", sum(w * values), "thousand euros\n")   # the book: 493
```

:::

The book's worked example (Section 11.2) makes the computation exact with three tokens and $d_k = 2$: Q, K and V are given, and four steps, scores, scaling, softmax, weighted sum, produce every number by hand. The figure below carries them out for one query at a time, with the scaling as a knob and the output drawn as what it is, a weighted average of the three value rows.

```{=html}
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('ix-attn'), L = window.LMIX, $ = s => root.querySelector(s);
  // The book's worked example (Section 11.2): three tokens, d_k = 2.
  const Q = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], K = [[1, 1], [0, 1], [1, 0]], V = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]];
  const S = Q.map(q => K.map(k => q[0] * k[0] + q[1] * k[1]));          // QK^T: scores
  const BOOK = 1 / Math.sqrt(2);                                         // the book's 1/sqrt(d_k)
  let s = BOOK, qi = 2, mask = false;
  function weights(i) {
    const z = S[i].map((v, j) => (mask && j > i) ? -Infinity : s * v);
    const mx = Math.max(...z), e = z.map(v => v === -Infinity ? 0 : Math.exp(v - mx)), t = e.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    return e.map(v => v / t);
  }
  const output = w => [0, 1].map(c => w.reduce((acc, wj, j) => acc + wj * V[j][c], 0));

  const td = (v, style) => '<td' + (style ? ' style="' + style + '"' : '') + '>' + v + '</td>';
  function matrices(C, w, o) {
    const hi = 'color:' + C.fs + ';font-weight:700';
    let h = '<span class="lhs">QK<sup>⊤</sup> =</span><table>';
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { h += '<tr>'; for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) h += td((mask && j > i) ? '<span style="color:' + C.muted + '">−∞</span>' : String(S[i][j]), i === qi ? hi : ''); h += '</tr>'; }
    $('.m-scores').innerHTML = h + '</table>';
    let g = '<span class="lhs">softmax(' + L.fmt(s, 2) + ' × row ' + (qi + 1) + ') =</span><table><tr>' + w.map(v => td(L.fmt(v, 2), 'color:' + C.fs)).join('') + '</tr></table>';
    g += '<span class="lhs">× V =</span><table><tr>' + o.map(v => td(L.fmt(v, 2), 'color:' + C.orange)).join('') + '</tr></table>';
    $('.m-weights').innerHTML = g;
  }
  const P = { x0: 46, x1: 386, y0: 16, y1: 326, X: [-0.15, 1.25], Y: [-0.15, 1.25] };
  const px = v => P.x0 + (v - P.X[0]) / (P.X[1] - P.X[0]) * (P.x1 - P.x0);
  const py = v => P.y1 - (v - P.Y[0]) / (P.Y[1] - P.Y[0]) * (P.y1 - P.y0);
  function plane(C, w, o) {
    const svg = $('.ix-plane'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    [0, 0.5, 1].forEach(v => {
      L.el('line', { x1: px(v), x2: px(v), y1: P.y0, y2: P.y1, stroke: v === 0 ? C.axis : C.grid }, svg);
      L.el('line', { x1: P.x0, x2: P.x1, y1: py(v), y2: py(v), stroke: v === 0 ? C.axis : C.grid }, svg);
      L.el('text', { x: px(v), y: P.y1 + 18, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v;
      L.el('text', { x: P.x0 - 7, y: py(v) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v;
    });
    L.el('polygon', { points: V.map(v => px(v[0]) + ',' + py(v[1])).join(' '), fill: C.plane, stroke: C.cyan, 'stroke-width': 1.2 }, svg);
    V.forEach((v, j) => L.el('line', { x1: px(v[0]), y1: py(v[1]), x2: px(o[0]), y2: py(o[1]), stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 0.5 + 9 * w[j], 'stroke-opacity': 0.55 }, svg));
    V.forEach((v, j) => {
      L.el('circle', { cx: px(v[0]), cy: py(v[1]), r: 7, fill: C.blue, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 2 }, svg);
      L.el('text', { x: px(v[0]) + (v[0] > 0.5 ? -12 : 12), y: py(v[1]) + (v[1] > 0.5 ? -10 : 22), 'text-anchor': v[0] > 0.5 ? 'end' : 'start', 'font-size': 16, 'font-style': 'italic', fill: C.blue }, svg).textContent = 'v' + (j + 1) + ' = (' + v[0] + ', ' + v[1] + ')';
    });
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(o[0]), cy: py(o[1]), r: 8, fill: C.orange, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 2 }, svg);
    L.el('text', { x: px(o[0]) + 12, y: py(o[1]) + 5, 'font-size': 15, fill: C.orange }, svg).textContent = 'output ' + (qi + 1);
  }
  const trio = w => '(' + w.map(v => L.fmt(v, 2)).join(', ') + ')';
  function note(w, o) {
    const big = Math.max(...w), who = w.indexOf(big) + 1;
    if (mask && qi === 0) return 'With the future masked, position 1 may attend only to itself: its weight on itself is 1 and its output is v₁ exactly. Nothing a later token carries can leak back.';
    if (mask && qi === 1) return 'With the future masked, position 2 sees positions 1 and 2 and splits its weight between them, ' + trio(w) + '. The output moves onto the edge between v₁ and v₂.';
    if (mask) return 'Position 3 sees everything, so the mask changes nothing for it: the weight matrix is lower triangular, and this is its full last row.';
    if (s < 0.02) return 'With s = 0 every score is the same, so the weights are 1/3 each for every query and every output is the centroid of the triangle, (0.67, 0.67). Attention has stopped attending.';
    if (Math.abs(s - BOOK) < 0.02 && qi === 2) return 'The book\'s scaling, 1/√2. Position 3\'s query (1, 1) scores 2 against position 1\'s key and 1 against the others, so after scaling and the softmax its weights are (0.50, 0.25, 0.25): half its output comes from v₁ = (1, 0), and the output lands at (0.75, 0.50), nearest v₁.';
    if (Math.abs(s - BOOK) < 0.02) return 'The book\'s scaling, 1/√2. Query ' + (qi + 1) + ' scores 1 against two keys and 0 against the third, so its weights are ' + trio(w) + ' and its output sits between the two values it favors.';
    if (s >= 3) return 'A large multiplier pushes the softmax toward a hard choice: the weight on the best-scoring key heads to 1 and the output heads to that value point' + (w.filter(v => Math.abs(v - big) < 1e-6).length > 1 ? ', except that this query scores two keys equally, so they share the weight and the output stops midway between them' : '') + '. The gradient of the softmax is all but gone up there.';
    return 'Multiplier ' + L.fmt(s, 2) + ': the weights are ' + trio(w) + ', the largest on position ' + who + '. Slide s up and the weights sharpen toward that position; slide it down and they flatten toward 1/3 each. The output never leaves the triangle.';
  }
  function update() {
    const C = L.colors(root), w = weights(qi), o = output(w);
    matrices(C, w, o); plane(C, w, o);
    L.stat($('.t-w'), 0, false, () => trio(w));
    L.stat($('.t-o'), 0, false, () => '(' + L.fmt(o[0], 2) + ', ' + L.fmt(o[1], 2) + ')');
    L.stat($('.t-m'), Math.max(...w), Math.max(...w) > 0.99, v => L.fmt(v, 2));
    [0, 1, 2].forEach(i => $('.q-' + i).classList.toggle('on', i === qi));
    $('.b-mask').classList.toggle('on', mask);
    $('.ix-note').textContent = note(w, o);
  }
  const sl = L.slider($('.ix-s'), $('.ix-sv'), v => L.fmt(v, 2), v => { s = v; update(); });
  const bar = $('.ix-buttons');
  L.presets(bar, [
    { label: 'Query 1', action: () => { qi = 0; update(); } },
    { label: 'Query 2', action: () => { qi = 1; update(); } },
    { label: 'Query 3', action: () => { qi = 2; update(); } },
    { label: 'Mask the future', action: () => { mask = !mask; update(); } },
  ]);
  [0, 1, 2].forEach(i => bar.children[i].classList.add('q-' + i)); bar.children[3].classList.add('b-mask');
  const gap = document.createElement('div'); gap.className = 'gap'; bar.appendChild(gap);
  L.presets(bar, [
    { label: 'The book\'s 1/√d_k (s = 0.71)', action: () => sl.set(BOOK) },
    { label: 'Raw scores (s = 1)', action: () => sl.set(1) },
    { label: 'Sharper (s = 4)', action: () => sl.set(4) },
    { label: 'Flat (s = 0)', action: () => sl.set(0) },
  ]);
  sl.refresh();
})();
</script>
</div>
```

## Attention by hand

Once Q, K, and V are in hand the mechanism is four lines of arithmetic, so it runs here rather than in Colab. The difficulty in a toy example is not the code but the embeddings. Random ones do not give a flat heatmap — the softmax finds peaks in noise readily enough — but the peaks correspond to nothing you can name, which teaches nothing. So we build the embeddings by hand. Each token is a one-hot vector over eight semantic roles — determiner, animate noun, object noun, verb, connective, property, pronoun, copula — and the query projection `W_Q` is a table saying what each role goes looking for. This extends the book's two-feature example, where `W_Q` maps the pronoun feature onto the noun feature so that *it* looks for nouns: a pronoun hunts an animate noun, a verb its arguments, a determiner a noun. Keys and values are left raw, so a score is read straight off that table. A trained model learns all of this; we are only writing down the answer in order to see the shape of it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Eight semantic roles. A real model learns its embeddings; we hand-build them so
# every number below can be read off the sentence.
ROLES = ["ANIMATE", "OBJECT", "DET", "VERB", "CONN", "PROP", "PRON", "COP"]
ROLE = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(ROLES)}
d_k = len(ROLES)

sentence = [("the", "DET"), ("cat", "ANIMATE"), ("drank", "VERB"),
            ("the", "DET"), ("milk", "OBJECT"), ("because", "CONN"),
            ("it", "PRON"), ("was", "COP"), ("thirsty", "PROP")]
tokens = [tok for tok, _ in sentence]
X = np.eye(d_k)[[ROLE[r] for _, r in sentence]]   # one-hot role embeddings

# The query projection is the only thing we shape: row r says what a token of
# role r goes looking for. Keys and values stay raw, so a score is read straight
# off this table.
W_Q = np.zeros((d_k, d_k))
W_Q[ROLE["ANIMATE"], ROLE["VERB"]] = 6.0      # a subject looks for its verb
W_Q[ROLE["ANIMATE"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 3.0
W_Q[ROLE["OBJECT"], ROLE["VERB"]] = 6.0       # so does an object
W_Q[ROLE["OBJECT"], ROLE["OBJECT"]] = 3.0
W_Q[ROLE["DET"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 5.0       # a determiner looks for a noun
W_Q[ROLE["DET"], ROLE["OBJECT"]] = 5.0
W_Q[ROLE["VERB"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 4.5      # a verb looks for its arguments
W_Q[ROLE["VERB"], ROLE["OBJECT"]] = 4.5
W_Q[ROLE["CONN"], ROLE["VERB"]] = 3.0         # a connective joins clause to clause
W_Q[ROLE["CONN"], ROLE["PROP"]] = 4.0
W_Q[ROLE["PROP"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 5.0      # a property looks for what it describes
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 8.0      # a pronoun hunts its referent
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"], ROLE["OBJECT"]] = 2.0
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"], ROLE["PROP"]] = 2.0
W_Q[ROLE["COP"], ROLE["PROP"]] = 5.0          # a copula links subject to property
W_Q[ROLE["COP"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] = 4.0
W_K = np.eye(d_k)
W_V = np.eye(d_k)

def softmax_rows(S):
    """Row-wise softmax. Subtracting the row max first keeps exp() from overflowing."""
    E = np.exp(S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return E / E.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

Q, K, V = X @ W_Q, X @ W_K, X @ W_V
scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)               # scaled query-key similarity
A = softmax_rows(scores)                      # the kernel weights (Nadaraya–Watson, Ch. 11)
context = A @ V                               # weighted average of the values

assert np.allclose(A.sum(axis=1), 1.0), "each row must be a distribution"
n = len(tokens)
print("attention weights (row attends to column)")
print(f"{'':>8} " + " ".join(f"{t:>7}" for t in tokens))
for i, t in enumerate(tokens):
    print(f"{t:>8} " + " ".join(f"{v:7.3f}" for v in A[i]))
print(f"\nrow sums: {np.round(A.sum(axis=1), 12)}")
print(f"'it' -> 'cat' {A[6, 1]:.3f}; next largest in that row {np.sort(A[6])[-2]:.3f}")
print(f"the two 'the' rows differ by at most {np.abs(A[0] - A[3]).max():.1e}")
unscaled = softmax_rows(Q @ K.T)
p, p_u = A.max(), unscaled.max()
print(f"largest weight anywhere: scaled {p:.3f}, unscaled {p_u:.3f}")
print(f"softmax slope p(1-p) there: scaled {p * (1 - p):.3f}, unscaled {p_u * (1 - p_u):.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 5.0))
im = ax.imshow(A, cmap="Blues", vmin=0.0, vmax=A.max())
cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.03)
cb.set_label("attention weight", fontsize=11)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)
cb.outline.set_edgecolor("#cfccc2")
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n):
        if A[i, j] >= 0.10:
            ax.text(j, i, f"{A[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                    color="white" if A[i, j] > 0.45 else "#31417A")
ax.set_xticks(range(n)); ax.set_xticklabels(tokens, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels(tokens)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, n, 1), minor=True)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, n, 1), minor=True)
ax.grid(which="minor", color="#e6e3da", lw=0.8)
ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)
ax.tick_params(colors="#666666", labelsize=10)
for s in ax.spines.values():
    s.set_color("#cfccc2")
ax.set_xlabel("key — token attended to", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel("query — token attending", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("context vector for 'it':", np.round(context[6], 3))
print("largest component:", ROLES[int(np.argmax(context[6]))])
```

## R
```{webr}
ROLES <- c("ANIMATE", "OBJECT", "DET", "VERB", "CONN", "PROP", "PRON", "COP")
ROLE <- setNames(seq_along(ROLES), ROLES)
d_k <- length(ROLES)

tokens <- c("the", "cat", "drank", "the", "milk", "because", "it", "was", "thirsty")
roles  <- c("DET", "ANIMATE", "VERB", "DET", "OBJECT", "CONN", "PRON", "COP", "PROP")
X <- diag(d_k)[ROLE[roles], ]                 # one-hot role embeddings

# The query projection is the only thing we shape: row r says what a token of
# role r goes looking for. Keys and values stay raw, so a score is read straight
# off this table.
W_Q <- matrix(0, d_k, d_k)
W_Q[ROLE["ANIMATE"], ROLE["VERB"]]    <- 6.0   # a subject looks for its verb
W_Q[ROLE["ANIMATE"], ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 3.0
W_Q[ROLE["OBJECT"],  ROLE["VERB"]]    <- 6.0   # so does an object
W_Q[ROLE["OBJECT"],  ROLE["OBJECT"]]  <- 3.0
W_Q[ROLE["DET"],     ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 5.0   # a determiner looks for a noun
W_Q[ROLE["DET"],     ROLE["OBJECT"]]  <- 5.0
W_Q[ROLE["VERB"],    ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 4.5   # a verb looks for its arguments
W_Q[ROLE["VERB"],    ROLE["OBJECT"]]  <- 4.5
W_Q[ROLE["CONN"],    ROLE["VERB"]]    <- 3.0   # a connective joins clause to clause
W_Q[ROLE["CONN"],    ROLE["PROP"]]    <- 4.0
W_Q[ROLE["PROP"],    ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 5.0   # a property looks for what it describes
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"],    ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 8.0   # a pronoun hunts its referent
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"],    ROLE["OBJECT"]]  <- 2.0
W_Q[ROLE["PRON"],    ROLE["PROP"]]    <- 2.0
W_Q[ROLE["COP"],     ROLE["PROP"]]    <- 5.0   # a copula links subject to property
W_Q[ROLE["COP"],     ROLE["ANIMATE"]] <- 4.0
W_K <- diag(d_k)
W_V <- diag(d_k)

# Row-wise softmax. Subtracting the row max first keeps exp() from overflowing.
softmax_rows <- function(S) {
  E <- exp(S - apply(S, 1, max))
  E / rowSums(E)
}

Q <- X %*% W_Q; K <- X %*% W_K; V <- X %*% W_V
scores <- Q %*% t(K) / sqrt(d_k)              # scaled query-key similarity
A <- softmax_rows(scores)                     # the kernel weights (Nadaraya–Watson, Ch. 11)
context <- A %*% V                            # weighted average of the values

stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(A) - 1) < 1e-12))
n <- length(tokens)
cat("attention weights (row attends to column)\n")
cat(sprintf("%8s ", ""), sprintf("%7s", tokens), "\n")
for (i in seq_len(n))
  cat(sprintf("%8s ", tokens[i]), sprintf("%7.3f", A[i, ]), "\n")
cat(sprintf("\nrow sums: %s\n", paste(sprintf("%.12f", rowSums(A)), collapse = " ")))
cat(sprintf("'it' -> 'cat' %.3f; next largest in that row %.3f\n",
            A[7, 2], sort(A[7, ], decreasing = TRUE)[2]))
cat(sprintf("the two 'the' rows differ by at most %.1e\n", max(abs(A[1, ] - A[4, ]))))
unscaled <- softmax_rows(Q %*% t(K))
p <- max(A); p_u <- max(unscaled)
cat(sprintf("largest weight anywhere: scaled %.3f, unscaled %.3f\n", p, p_u))
cat(sprintf("softmax slope p(1-p) there: scaled %.3f, unscaled %.4f\n",
            p * (1 - p), p_u * (1 - p_u)))

# image() lays z out column-by-column from the bottom left, so flip the rows to
# put token 1 at the top and match the Python panel.
blues <- colorRampPalette(c("#f7fbff", "#deebf7", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1",
                            "#6baed6", "#4292c6", "#2171b5", "#08519c", "#08306b"))
op <- par(mar = c(6.5, 6.5, 1.5, 1.5))
image(1:n, 1:n, t(A[n:1, ]), col = blues(100), zlim = c(0, max(A)),
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = 1:n, labels = tokens, las = 2, col = "#cfccc2", col.axis = "#666666")
axis(2, at = 1:n, labels = rev(tokens), las = 1, col = "#cfccc2", col.axis = "#666666")
box(col = "#cfccc2")
abline(v = seq(0.5, n + 0.5, 1), h = seq(0.5, n + 0.5, 1), col = "#e6e3da", lwd = 0.8)
mtext("key - token attended to", side = 1, line = 5)
mtext("query - token attending", side = 2, line = 5)
for (i in seq_len(n)) for (j in seq_len(n)) if (A[i, j] >= 0.10)
  text(j, n + 1 - i, sprintf("%.2f", A[i, j]), cex = 0.7,
       col = if (A[i, j] > 0.45) "white" else "#31417A")
par(op)

cat(sprintf("context vector for 'it': %s\n",
            paste(sprintf("%.3f", context[7, ]), collapse = " ")))
cat(sprintf("largest component: %s\n", ROLES[which.max(context[7, ])]))
```

:::

Five things in that output are worth reading off carefully.

The pronoun finds its referent. The row for `it` puts 0.627 on `cat` — more than eight times the 0.075 it gives anything else. Its output inherits that: the context vector for `it` comes out 0.627 along the animate axis and no more than 0.075 along any other, so a position that arrived carrying only "pronoun" leaves carrying "cat."

Predicate and arguments find each other. `cat` and `milk` each place 0.458 on `drank`, and `drank` splits 0.292 and 0.292 back between them. The link is visible in both directions but not with equal strength: attention is not symmetric, because each row is normalized on its own.

The floor is not zero. Every cell the query does not seek still holds between 0.037 and 0.072. A softmax cannot assign zero to a finite score, which is why the causal mask below sets future scores to $-\infty$ rather than to something merely small: only $-\infty$ exponentiates to exactly zero.

Nor is any row self-heavy. Self-preference was built in for two roles — `W_Q[ANIMATE, ANIMATE]` and `W_Q[OBJECT, OBJECT]` are both 3.0, and `cat` and `milk` duly give themselves 0.158, nearly three times the floor — but 3.0 loses to the 6.0 that sends both of them to `drank` at 0.458. No row's largest entry lies on the diagonal. Attention is not obliged to be self-heavy; here the preference was written in and outbid.

Position is missing. The two `the` rows are identical — the printed difference is exactly `0.0e+00`. That is not rounding; the two tokens have the same embedding, so the computation cannot tell them apart. Self-attention sees a set. Restoring the order is the job of the positional encoding described below.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}

Edit `sentence` and rerun. Change `("it", "PRON")` to `("it", "OBJECT")` and the pronoun's row swings off `cat` onto `drank` at 0.415, because object nouns are wired to seek verbs. Put a second animate noun in the sentence — insert `("and", "CONN"), ("dog", "ANIMATE")` after `("milk", "OBJECT")` — and `it` splits 0.377 and 0.377 between `cat` and `dog`, which is exactly the ambiguity a real coreference model has to resolve. Then scale the whole table down, `W_Q = 0.25 * W_Q`: every weight collapses into the band 0.096 to 0.195 around the uniform 1/9 = 0.111. The pattern was never in the softmax; it was in the size of the scores.
:::

## Why divide by &radic;d<sub>k</sub>

The division by &radic;d<sub>k</sub> is not cosmetic. Large scores push the softmax into a saturated region where its gradient all but vanishes, and the cell above prints what that costs on this very small example: the largest weight anywhere is 0.627 with the scaling and 0.993 without it. That second number is a hard argmax in all but name, and the softmax's own slope, p(1&minus;p), falls with it from 0.234 to 0.0069, a factor of thirty-four. Dividing by &radic;8 = 2.83 is the whole of the difference.

Where the dimension enters is a separate argument, and it carries a condition. If the components of a query and a key are independent, mean zero, and unit variance, then q&middot;k is a sum of d<sub>k</sub> independent products, so its variance is d<sub>k</sub> and its typical size grows like &radic;d<sub>k</sub>: the wider the head, the deeper into saturation an unscaled softmax goes. Dividing by &radic;d<sub>k</sub> restores unit variance whatever the width.

Our embeddings do not meet that condition, and it is worth being plain about it. The keys are one-hot and `W_Q` is a table we wrote down, so every score is a single entry of that table and does not vary with d<sub>k</sub> at all. Pad the roles out to d<sub>k</sub> = 512 and the unscaled maximum weight sits at 0.993 for every width, while the scaled one drifts down toward the uniform 1/9 — here the scaling over-corrects, because there was no growth to correct. So read the cell as a demonstration of the remedy rather than of the disease: it shows what saturation costs and that the division relieves it. Seeing the disease itself takes random projections, where the scores really do grow with the width.

## The same layer in PyTorch

From Chapter 9 onward the models are built in PyTorch, which wants a numerical stack and ideally a GPU, more than a browser sandbox can carry; one click opens the full notebook on Google's free hardware with no local install.

```{=html}
<a class="colab-btn" href="https://colab.research.google.com/github/welr/learning_machines/blob/main/ch11_01_attention_transformers.ipynb" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span class="dot"></span> Open in Google Colab</a>
```

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    """Q, K, V: (..., seq_len, d_k). Returns context vectors and attention weights."""
    d_k = Q.size(-1)
    scores = (Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)) / d_k ** 0.5   # query–key similarity
    if mask is not None:                              # causal mask: no peeking ahead
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
    weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)               # the kernel weights (Nadaraya–Watson, Ch. 11)
    context = weights @ V                             # weighted average of the values
    return context, weights
```

This is the cell above with the projections learned rather than written down, batching added, and the mask made available. The arithmetic is unchanged.

## Multi-head attention

A single head captures one kind of relationship. [Multi-head attention]{.term} runs several heads in parallel, each with its own learned projections, then concatenates their outputs and projects once more. Different heads specialize: in a trained model one may track syntactic agreement while another links a pronoun to its referent. The notebook builds the multi-head layer from the function above, splitting the model dimension across heads so the parallel attention costs no more than a single wide one.

## Position and causality

Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: it treats its input as a set, not a sequence, so on its own it cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog." The two identical `the` rows in the heatmap above are that fact in miniature. Position is restored by adding a [positional encoding]{.term} to each embedding. The original transformer uses sinusoids of geometrically spaced frequencies, where low dimensions oscillate quickly to mark local position and high dimensions slowly to mark global position, and relative offsets become linear combinations of the encodings.

Autoregressive models such as GPT carry one more constraint. When predicting the next token, a position must attend only to those before it, never ahead. A [causal mask]{.term}, the lower-triangular pattern passed to `masked_fill` above, sets every future score to negative infinity before the softmax, so position t draws on positions 1 through t alone. This is what lets the model be trained on all positions at once without leaking the answer.

## A transformer block

The block wraps two sublayers. First comes multi-head self-attention, added back to its input through a [residual connection]{.term} and stabilized by [layer normalization]{.term}; then a position-wise feed-forward network, again with a residual and a norm. Residuals add an identity route for gradients, and layer norm holds the distribution of activations steady as they pass through the depth. In this ordering, though, the norm sits on the residual path itself, so the identity route passes through every LayerNorm; Exercise 4(a) of Chapter 11 asks why that stops the sublayer from passing gradients unchanged.

```python
import torch.nn as nn

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    """Multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network,
    each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads)   # h heads in parallel
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ff = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),
        )
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        attn_out, weights = self.attention(x, mask)
        x = self.norm1(x + self.dropout(attn_out))    # attention, residual, norm
        ff_out = self.ff(x)
        x = self.norm2(x + self.dropout(ff_out))      # feed-forward, residual, norm
        return x, weights
```

Here `MultiHeadAttention` is the layer the notebook builds around `scaled_dot_product_attention`. Nothing in the block would surprise a reader who understood kernel smoothing and the gradient descent of Chapter 3; the transformer is those ideas, made deep and made trainable. Stacking many such blocks gives the architecture that Chapter 12 turns into a language model.

The order above is the book's Equations 11.5 and 11.6: each sublayer is applied, added to its
input, and then normalized. This is the *post-LN* arrangement. The Chapter 12 capstone uses the
*pre-LN* arrangement instead, normalizing before each sublayer and leaving the residual path
clear, which trains more stably at depth. They are two orderings of the same three components,
and the book notes the difference in a footnote to Section 11.3.

One cost is worth naming. Because every token attends to every other, attention is O(n&sup2;) in sequence length n: a thousand-token sequence means roughly a million pairwise scores per layer. That quadratic scaling motivates sparse and linear variants, cheaper approximations that give up some of attention's direct access to distant positions. (FlashAttention is a different answer: it computes attention exactly, still with n&sup2; arithmetic, and saves by reducing memory traffic.) Standard attention remains the right default for the moderate sequence lengths most applications use.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}

In Colab, set `Q = K = V` and run attention with the projections frozen to the identity. With a fixed, un-learned similarity the layer reduces exactly to a Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoother; a learned similarity is the whole of what attention adds.
:::
